name: Anti-Caro: Fantasy Variation
pgn: e4 c6 d4 d5 f3 dxe4 fxe4 e5 Nf3 Bg4 c3 Nd7 Bd3 Ngf6 O-O Bd6 a4 O-O Nbd2 Re8 Qc2 Bc7
uci: e2e4 c7c6 d2d4 d7d5 f2f3 e7e6 b1c3 f8b4 c1f4 c6c5 a2a3 c5c4 b2b3 e6e5
overview: The Fantasy Variation, 3.f3, is a surprise weapon against the Caro-Kann. Be honest: it is not a refutation — with best play it is roughly equal. Its value is practical: f3 props up e4 and builds a broad d4+e4 pawn centre, dragging the well-booked Caro player off theory and into a rich middlegame where they, not you, must find the moves. Club opponents stumble in it constantly.
keyIdeas: After ...dxe4 recapture with fxe4 — the broad d4+e4 centre and the half-open f-file are the whole point.
Bolt down d4 with c3 and Nf3 so Black's ...e5 break never wins the centre.
Develop the Bd3+Qc2 battery on the b1-h7 diagonal, poised to fire at the king once the e4-pawn advances.
It is a practical weapon, not a refutation — play for the small pull and Black's unfamiliarity, and mine the amateur blunders (…c5, …c4) as tactics.

pgn: e4 e6 d4 d5 e5 c5 c3 Nc6 Nf3 Qb6 Be2 cxd4 cxd4 Nh6 Bd3 Bd7 Bc2 Nf5 Bxf5 exf5 O-O Be6

overview: The Advance Variation, 3.e5, is White's most principled counter to the French. You grab space with the e5 wedge and lock in Black's light-squared bishop behind its own e6-pawn — the bad piece that plagues the whole French complex. Your plan is simple and enduring: defend the d4 base of the pawn chain (c3, Nf3, Be2), keep your good light bishop, and squeeze the extra space. A clean, thematic edge with well-charted plans.
keyIdeas: The e5 wedge grabs space and buries Black's light-squared bishop behind the e6-pawn — the French's eternal problem.
Hold the d4 base of the chain with c3, Nf3 and Be2 against the ...c5/...Nc6/...Qb6 pressure.
Keep your good bishop: reposition Bd3-c2 onto the b1-h7 diagonal instead of trading it cheaply.
When Black blockades with ...Nf5, trade it with Bxf5 — the recapture ...exf5 hands Black doubled f-pawns.

overview: The Austrian Attack is the sharpest weapon against the Pirc: a towering e4-d4-f4 pawn front backing a direct kingside attack. Develop the pieces toward Black's king (Nf3, Bd3), and when Black counters in the centre with ...c5/...c4/...b5, accurate grabs (Bxc4, Nxb5) turn his charging pawns into targets and leave you a clean pawn up.
keyIdeas: Grab space and attacking potential with the big e4-d4-f4 pawn front.
Aim the pieces kingside — Nf3 toward e5/g5, Bd3 on the b1-h7 diagonal.
Meet ...c5 with d5, keeping the front intact and gaining more space.
Answer the ...c4/...b5 counter accurately — Bxc4 and Nxb5 win pawns; Qe1 parries ...Nxe4.

name: Anti-Pirc: 150 Battery & d5 Squeeze
pgn: e4 d6 d4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Nf3 Bg7 Be3 O-O Qd2 Nc6 d5 Nb8 Bh6 c6 Bxg7 Kxg7 a3 Nbd7 O-O-O cxd5 exd5 Nb6 Re1 Bd7 Ng5 Rc8
uci: e2e4 d7d6 d2d4 g8f6 b1c3 g7g6 g1f3 f8g7 c1e3 e8g8 d1d2 b8c6 d4d5 c6b8 e3h6 c7c6 h6g7 g8g7 a2a3 b8d7 e1c1 c6d5 e4d5 d7b6 d1e1 c8d7 f3g5 a8c8
overview: The professional recipe against the Pirc and Modern: take the full centre, stack the Be3+Qd2 dark-square battery with the knight on f3, and the moment Black castles and commits a knight to c6, punch d5 — gaining space and sending the knight all the way home. Then Bh6 trades off the fianchetto bishop, a quiet a3 takes b4 away forever, and White castles long into a comfortable, engine-approved squeeze. Positional pressure with an attacker's payoff.
keyIdeas: Stack the Be3 + Qd2 battery early — Bh6 hangs over every Black plan.
The moment Black castles and plays the knight to c6, punch d5 and gain space.
Trade the g7 bishop with Bh6 — the dark squares around the king never recover.
Prophylactic a3 before castling long: deny b4, then squeeze on the open e-file.

variations.name: Punishing …Ng4
variations.pgn: e4 d6 d4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 Nf3 Bg7 Be3 O-O Qd2 Ng4 Bg5 h6 Bh4 g5 Bg3 e5 dxe5 dxe5 h4
variations.explanation: The knight hop to g4 looks annoying but wins nothing: meet it with Bg5, and after …h6 and …g5 the bishop slides to g3 while Black has permanently loosened g5 and h6. Later h4 rips those weaknesses open — the engine already gives White better than a pawn's worth of pressure.

variations.name: The …e5 Endgame Grind
variations.pgn: e4 d6 d4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 dxe5 dxe5 Qxd8+ Kxd8 f4 Bb4 Bd2 exf4 O-O-O Bg4 Nf3 Nbd7 Bxf4 Bxc3 bxc3
variations.explanation: When Black meets the centre with …e5 instead of the fianchetto, trade into the queenless middlegame: the king is stuck in the centre with castling rights gone, and f4 pries the position open. Objectively balanced — but across 141 corpus games this grind scores 66 percent for White, because every practical problem belongs to Black.

variations.name: Modern Order: the Gurgenidze …c6+…d5

variations.explanation: Via the Modern move order Black sometimes strikes with …c6 and …d5. Hold the centre with f3, and when the tension resolves the engine gives White nearly two pawns of advantage in the resulting queenless position — the lead in development and the open d-file do the scoring. 274 corpus games in this structure back it up.

name: Anti-Scandinavian: Main Line
pgn: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qa5 d4 Nf6 Nf3 c6 Bc4 Bf5 Bd2 e6 Ne4 Qd8 Ng3 Bg4 c3 Nbd7 h3 Bxf3
uci: e2e4 d7d5 e4d5 d8d5 b1c3 d5a5 d2d4 g8f6 g1f3 c7c6 f1c4 c8f5
overview: Against the Scandinavian (1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5), White's edge is time. Because Black recaptures with the queen so early, every developing move you make comes with a threat to it: Nc3, then Ne4 and Ng3 harry Black's forces while you build a big centre and finish development for free. You emerge with the bishop pair, more space, and a clear lead in development — a clean, low-maintenance plus.
keyIdeas: Develop with tempo — Nc3 hits the queen; every queen move Black makes is a move you spend building.
Stake out the centre with d4 and post the bishop actively on c4, eyeing f7.
Harry the pieces with Ne4 and Ng3, driving the knight and bishop to worse squares while gaining time.
Bank the bishop pair and the development lead — a comfortable, risk-free edge to convert.

trapLines.name: Scandinavian Bishop Trap (…Qh5?)
trapLines.pgn: e4 d5 exd5 Qxd5 Nc3 Qa5 d4 Nf6 Nf3 Bg4 h3 Qh5 hxg4 Qxg4 Rh4
trapLines.explanation: In the main-line Scandinavian, after 6.h3 attacks the g4-bishop, Black's natural-looking …Qh5 tries to keep the pin by defending the bishop with the queen. It's a blunder played in tens of thousands of amateur games: hxg4 simply wins the bishop, and after …Qxg4 the rook lift Rh4 hunts the queen while White stays up a clean piece. Engine-verified crushing (about +5.8). Punish the greedy queen.

overview: Against the Alekhine, the Modern/Exchange approach takes the space Black offers: e5 and d4 build a broad centre, c4 gains more and chases the knight to the rim, and calm development banks the space plus a lead in development. Low theory, a lasting pull.
keyIdeas: Grab the big e5+d4 centre the Alekhine dares you to build, then support it.
c4 gains space and kicks the d5-knight back to the passive b6.
Develop calmly (Nf3, Be2, O-O) — the Modern line is a slow squeeze, not a shootout.
Bank the space and development lead against Black's backward d6-pawn.

pgn: e4 g6 d4 Bg7 Nc3 d6 Be3 a6 Qd2 Nf6 f3 O-O O-O-O Nc6 Nd5 a5 Nxf6+ exf6 h4 f5 h5 fxe4

overview: The 150 Attack is the classic anti-fianchetto recipe against the Modern and Pirc: build the Be3/Qd2 battery, play f3 to make the centre granite, castle queenside, and storm the kingside with h4-h5 while trading off Black's dark-squared bishop. Direct, thematic, and brutally effective against passive play.
keyIdeas: Build the Be3 + Qd2 battery, aiming Bh6 to trade Black's fianchettoed bishop.
Play f3 to bolt down e4 and free the g- and h-pawns to storm.
Castle queenside and roll h4-h5 into the fianchetto while Black's counterplay lags.
Use the Nd5 outpost and Nxf6+ to shatter Black's kingside pawns and open lines.

name: Anti-Sicilian: Rossolimo
pgn: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 g6 O-O Bg7 Re1 Nf6 e5 Nd5 Nc3 Nc7 Bxc6 dxc6 Ne4 Ne6 d3 O-O Be3 b6 Qd2 Nd4 Nxd4 cxd4 Bh6 c5

overview: The Rossolimo, 3.Bb5, is White's low-theory antidote to the Sicilian's ...Nc6 lines. Rather than memorise Najdorf mainlines, White trades the light bishop for the c6-knight, saddles Black with doubled c-pawns or a cramped structure, and plays a clean positional game for the bishop pair, central space, and the better pawns. It scores heavily at club level because it sidesteps Black's preparation and steers into positions of pure understanding.
keyIdeas: Bxc6 at the right moment doubles Black's pawns on the c-file — the permanent structural target the whole middlegame is built on against the ...g6 fianchetto.
Against ...e6 and ...d6, retreat the bishop to f1 instead of trading — keep the bishop pair and build a d4/c4 space clamp.
The e4-e5 space grab and the knight outpost on e4 cramp Black and rob the ...g6 lines of counterplay.
Trade off Black's fianchettoed dark-squared bishop with Be3-h6 to leave holes around the king; you play for two results with no risk.

pgn: d4 Nf6 c4 c5 d5 b5 cxb5 a6 bxa6 Bxa6 Nc3 d6 Nf3 g6 e4 Bxf1 Kxf1 Bg7 g3 O-O Kg2 Nbd7
uci: d2d4 g8f6 c2c4 c7c5 d4d5 b7b5 c4b5 a7a6 b5a6 c8a6 b1c3 d7d6 g1f3 g7g6 e2e4 a6f1 e1f1 f8g7 g2g3 e8g8 f1g2 b8d7
overview: Against the Benoni push Black offers the Benko/Volga pawn with ...b5, sacrificing for slow queenside pressure on the a- and b-files. The soundest answer is the most direct: take it cleanly with cxb5 and give the square back with bxa6 so Black recaptures with the bishop. Then build a big e4 centre, trade the light bishops, and walk the king to g2 by hand. Engine-verified a healthy pawn up (+0.93) with the Benko's counterplay defused.
keyIdeas: Accept the gambit: cxb5, then bxa6 so Black recaptures with the bishop, not a rook-file.
Raise a broad e4/d5 pawn front to wall off Black's queenside counterplay.
Trade the light bishops (Bxf1 Kxf1) and finish the king by hand with g3 and Kg2.
Keep the extra pawn and convert patiently — the Benko pressure never crashes through.

pgn: d4 e5 dxe5 Nc6 Nf3 Qe7 Bf4 Qb4+ Bd2 Qxb2 Nc3 Bb4 Rb1 Qa3 Nd5 Ba5 Rb5 Bxd2+ Qxd2 Rb8 c3 a6

overview: The Englund Gambit (1.d4 e5) throws a pawn away for cheap tricks and is simply unsound. You take the pawn, guard it with Nf3 and Bf4, and when Black lashes out with ...Qb4+ and grabs a second pawn on b2, you spring the trap: Nc3, Rb1 and Nd5/Rb5 hunt the greedy queen down on the rim. Engine-verified winning for White (+1.97) — greed punished by a clean queen hunt.
keyIdeas: Take the e5-pawn and hold it simply — Nf3 guards, Bf4 develops and defends.
Let Black overreach: ...Qb4+ and ...Qxb2 sends the queen pawn-hunting into your camp.
Spring the net with Nc3 and Rb1 — every developing move also chases the queen.
Finish with Nd5 and Rb5, boxing the queen on the edge — winning material by force.

trapLines.pgn: d4 e5 dxe5 Nc6 Nf3 Qe7 Bf4 Qb4+ Bd2 Qxb2 Nc3 Bb4 Rb1 Qa3 Nd5 Ba5 Rb5

White emerges winning by a wide margin — engine-verified about +2.2. Greed punished by a clean hunt.

keyIdeas: f3 supports e4 and lets you build the biggest centre in chess — c4, d4 and e4.
Meet ...e5 with d5, the Sämisch clamp that cramps Black on both wings.
Keep the good bishop (Bd3-c2) and grab the half-open c-file after ...c6 cxd5.
Play for Qd2 and a g4-h4 kingside pawn storm behind the space bind.

keyIdeas: Build the classical c3-d4-e4 phalanx after bxc3 — the Grünfeld's challenge to meet head-on.
Develop Ne2 (not Nf3) so the g7-bishop can't pin it, keeping d4 defended.
Over-defend the centre with Be3 and castle; it is defended as often as it is hit.
Answer ...Bg4 and ...Na5 with f3 — one move that kicks the bishop and cements e4.

Be honest — the Nimzo is a top defence and this is roughly level; the two bishops are your small, lasting edge.
keyIdeas: Qc2 defends c3 so ...Bxc3+ is met by Qxc3 — no doubled pawns, and you win the bishop pair.
Prod with a3 to invite the trade on your terms.
Clamp e4 with f3 and Bg5, preparing the broad centre your bishops crave.
It is roughly equal — play the two bishops for a riskless, long-game pull.

Defend c4 with b3 so the a6-bishop bites on granite.
Place both bishops on their long diagonals (Bg2 light, Bc3 dark) for a harmonious build.
Break with e4 to open the position for your bishops when Black plays ...d5.

uci: d2d4 f7f5 e2e4 f5e4 b1c3 g8f6 c1g5 c7c6 f2f3 d7d5 f3e4 f6e4 c3e4 d5e4 f1c4 d8d6 c2c3 d6g6 d1d2 c8f5 g1e2 b8d7
overview: The Staunton Gambit meets the Dutch with 2.e4, sacrificing a pawn to blow the position open before Black is developed. Bg5 hits the f6-knight and threatens to wreck the kingside; f3 undermines the extra e4-pawn at its base; Bc4 rakes the diagonal at Black's airy king. Objectively about level, but a dangerous practical surprise weapon — engine-verified with active, pleasant compensation (+0.25) and a fragile black e4-pawn to round up.
keyIdeas: Gambit e4 to rip open lines against the loosened Dutch king.
Bg5 hits f6 and threatens Bxf6 to shatter Black's kingside pawns.
Undermine the extra e4-pawn with f3 — it is weak and destined to fall.
Rake the a2-g8 diagonal with Bc4 and regroup Qd2/Ne2 to win the pawn back with the initiative.

overview: The Exchange Variation gives the Queen's Gambit Declined a clear, classical plan: the Carlsbad structure and the minority attack. You trade on d5, develop with Bg5 and Bd3, and push b4-b5 to fix a weak, backward pawn on c6 that you besiege for the rest of the game. Low-risk, high-clarity.
keyIdeas: Take on d5 for the Carlsbad structure and the famous minority-attack plan (b4-b5).
Pin with Bg5 and pressure d5; Black's ...c6 becomes your target.
Post the bishop on d3 aiming at the king and plant a knight on e5.
Choose your squeeze: the queenside minority attack or a kingside build behind the e5-knight.

pgn: d4 Nf6 c4 e5 dxe5 Ng4 Bf4 Nc6 Nf3 Bb4+ Nbd2 Qe7 e3 Ngxe5 Nxe5 Nxe5 a3 Bxd2+ Qxd2 d6 Be2 O-O

overview: The Budapest Gambit sacrifices the e5-pawn and chases it with ...Ng4. The critical, greed-free reply is 4.Bf4: it defends the extra pawn a second time AND develops — no h3/Nf3 tangles. Black regains the pawn by force, but a well-timed a3 wins the two bishops, and you emerge with the bishop pair, a healthy central pawn and the freer game. Engine-verified a small, durable edge (+0.35).
keyIdeas: Meet ...Ng4 with the clean Bf4 — defend e5 and develop, never cling greedily.
Answer ...Bb4+ with Nbd2, developing rather than retreating, and shore up with e3.
Win the bishop pair with a3 once Black regains the pawn (Bxd2+ Qxd2).
Nurse the two bishops and the c4-pawn for a small, lasting pull.

name: Anti-London (Black)
pgn: d4 d5 Bf4 Nf6 e3 Bf5 c4 e6 Nd2 Nbd7 Ngf3 a5 Be2 c6 Qb3 Ra7 c5 Be7 O-O Nh5 Be5 Nhf6
uci: d2d4 d7d5 c1f4 c7c5 e2e3 b8c6 c2c3 c5c4 a2a3 a7a6 b2b3 a6a5 f2f3 a5a4
overview: The London System's whole edge is its good bishop on f4, developed outside the pawn chain. You neutralise it at the root by mirroring: ...Nf6 and ...Bf5 to get your own light-squared bishop out BEFORE ...e6 shuts it in — the same principle that makes the Caro-Kann rock-solid. From a healthy setup the ...c5 break gives full equality. Be honest: the London is sound, so this is level, but Black has no problems and the freer minor pieces.
keyIdeas: Develop ...Bf5 before ...e6 — copy the London's idea and take away its one trump, the good bishop.
Only then play ...e6: your light bishop is already active outside the chain.
Grab space with ...a5 and prepare the freeing ...c5 break — play actively, not passively.
Reach a level game with both bishops good, no weaknesses, and the ...c5/...b6 breaks in hand.

pgn: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 g3 d5 Bg2 dxc4 Nf3 a6 O-O Nc6 e3 Bd7 Qe2 Bd6 Qxc4 O-O Rd1 Qe7 Nc3 h6

overview: Against the Catalan, the Open with ...dxc4 is Black's soundest, most reliable equaliser. You take the c4-pawn, hold it a moment with ...a6, and use the tempo White spends recovering it to develop every piece to a natural square. The result is a comfortable, level game with nothing for the fianchettoed bishop to squeeze.
keyIdeas: Take on c4 — grabbing the pawn clears the tension and buys you time.
Play ...a6 to threaten ...b5 so White must work to regain the pawn.
Develop naturally (...Nc6, ...Bd7, ...Bd6) while White fusses over c4.
Reach full equality with no weaknesses and the Catalan bishop neutralised.

name: Anti-Trompowsky: 2…Ne4 (Black)
pgn: d4 Nf6 Bg5 Ne4 Bf4 d5 e3 c5 Nd2 Nxd2 Qxd2 Nc6 Nf3 cxd4 exd4 Bf5 Bd3 Bxd3 Qxd3 e6 O-O Bd6
uci: d2d4 g8f6 c1g5 f6e4 g5f4 d7d5 e2e3 c7c5 b1d2 e4d2 d1d2 b8c6 g1f3 c5d4 e3d4 c8f5 f1d3 f5d3 d2d3 e7e6 e1g1 f8d6
overview: The Trompowsky's Bg5 wants to trade for your f6-knight and hand you doubled pawns. You refuse at the root with 2...Ne4 — the knight leaps to the centre, hits the bishop and dodges the pin. From there ...d5/...c5 stake a big centre, an active ...Bf5 frees your light bishop OUTSIDE the pawn chain before ...e6, and ...Bd6 challenges the last active enemy piece. Engine-verified dead level (-0.18) — the surprise met by pure principle.
keyIdeas: Refuse the pin with 2...Ne4 — jump to the centre and hit the bishop.
Stake a big centre with ...d5 and ...c5; after ...cxd4 exd4 White has a lone d-pawn to mind.
Free the good bishop with ...Bf5 before ...e6 ever locks it in — the Caro-Kann principle.
Challenge the dark-squared bishop with ...Bd6 and reach a symmetrical, equal game.

pgn: d4 d5 Nf3 Nf6 e3 c5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nc6 a3 a6 dxc5 Bxc5 b4 Bd6 cxd5 exd5 Bb2 Be6 Be2 O-O

keyIdeas: Strike with ...c5 at once — deny the Colle its cosy e3/Bd3/c3 bind.
Develop actively (...e6, ...Nc6, ...Bd6) into an open Queen's-Gambit-style game.
Welcome trades — every exchange frees your position against a cramping system.
Reach an equal middlegame with the freer, easier side to play.

overview: The soundest way to meet the Smith-Morra Gambit is to accept the pawn and consolidate. The ...a6/...e6/...Nge7 wall blunts White's development lead move by move: ...e6 shuts the c4-bishop, ...a6 and ...b5 gain queenside space, and ...Nge7 keeps the knight unpinned. Be honest — White has real compensation and it is roughly level, but with careful play the extra pawn tells.
keyIdeas: Accept the pawn — it is real, and White's compensation is manageable with a plan.
Build the ...e6/...a6/...Nge7 wall that defuses White's attack piece by piece.
Answer Bg5 with ...f6 and keep the dark squares solid.
Expand with ...b5 and ...Bb7, absorb the initiative, and let the extra pawn count.

pgn: e4 c5 c3 Nf6 e5 Nd5 d4 cxd4 Nf3 Nc6 cxd4 d6 Bc4 Nb6 Bb5 dxe5 Nxe5 Bd7 Nxd7 Qxd7 O-O e6
uci: e2e4 c7c5 c2c3 g8f6 e4e5 f6d5 d2d4 c5d4 g1f3 b8c6 c3d4 d7d6 a2a3 a7a6
overview: Against the Alapin (2.c3), ...Nf6 is the most testing reply: it hits e4 immediately and forces White to commit before completing his big-centre setup. After e5 the knight sits proudly on d5, you chip at the centre with ...cxd4 and ...Nc6, and the freeing ...d6 dissolves White's space edge into a comfortable, equal game.
keyIdeas: Meet 2.c3 with ...Nf6, attacking e4 and dictating the tempo.
After e5 Nd5, strike the centre with ...cxd4 and develop ...Nc6.
Play ...d6 to challenge the cramping e5-pawn and free your position.
Trade into equality with the isolated d4-pawn as a long-term target.

pgn: e4 c5 Nc3 Nc6 f4 g6 Nf3 Bg7 Bc4 e6 f5 Nge7 fxe6 dxe6 d3 O-O O-O h6 a4 b6 Ne2 Na5

overview: The Grand Prix Attack (f4) aims for a kingside mating attack, but the fianchetto defence takes all the sting out of it. ...g6 and ...Bg7 shield your king, ...e6 blunts the c4-bishop and the f5 break, and ...Na5 trades off White's most dangerous piece. Handled this way, Black is not just safe — Black is better.
keyIdeas: Fianchetto with ...g6/...Bg7 to guard the dark squares around your king.
Play ...e6 to shut the c4-bishop's diagonal and control f5.
Meet the f5 thrust calmly with ...Nge7 and recapture toward the centre.
Hit the c4-bishop with ...Na5 and take over — the attack has spent itself.

name: Belgrade Gambit (vs 1…e5)
pgn: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 d4 exd4 Nd5 Be7 Bd3 O-O O-O d6 h3 Nxd5 exd5 Ne5 Nxd4 Nxd3 Qxd3 Bf6 c4 b6 Re1 Re8 Bd2
uci: e2e4 e7e5 g1f3 b8c6 b1c3 g8f6 d2d4 e5d4 c3d5 f8e7 f1d3 e8g8 e1g1 d7d6 h2h3 f6d5 e4d5 c6e5 f3d4 e5d3 d1d3 e7f6 c2c4 b7b6 f1e1 f8e8 c1d2
overview: A surprise weapon against 1…e5 that most opponents will meet for the first time at the board: the Four Knights Scotch with the knight leap to d5 instead of the recapture. The old treatments deserved their bad reputation — the modern, engine-checked handling (the quiet Bd3, the calm regain, the d5 wedge) is fully sound, and the practical sting is real: 70.9 percent across 158 corpus games, with wins over elite opposition. Objectively level; practically venomous.
keyIdeas: Nd5 poses six different problems at once — most opponents have never seen one of them.
The modern move is the quiet Bd3: develop, castle, and regain d4 on your terms.
Every trade on d5 is met by exd5, kicking the c6-knight and gaining space.
The d5 wedge plus c4 plus the open e-file is the winning middlegame plan.

variations.name: The Greedy …Ne5 Refuted
variations.pgn: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 d4 exd4 Nd5 Nxd5 exd5 Ne5 Nxe5 Bb4+ Bd2 Qe7 Qe2 Bxd2+ Kxd2 Qg5+ Kd1 O-O
variations.explanation: After the early simplification on d5, hopping the knight to e5 to hold the extra pawn is the natural move — and it loses a piece. Take on e5, absorb the bishop check with the bishop, and the e-file check-and-fork machinery leaves White simply up material: the engine calls it nearly four pawns. This is the trap the whole gambit fishes for.

variations.name: The …Nxe4 Grab
variations.pgn: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 d4 exd4 Nd5 Nxe4 Bd3 Nc5 O-O Ne6 Re1 h6 Bf4 d6 Bg3 Ne7 Nf4 Nxf4
variations.explanation: Grabbing a second pawn with the knight is the critical test — and the most dangerous thing Black can do to himself at human speed. Develop with tempo against the wandering knight, castle, and take the open lines: the engine calls the position balanced, but every practical problem for the next ten moves belongs to Black.

variations.name: The …Nb4 Book Move
variations.pgn: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 d4 exd4 Nd5 Nb4 Nxf6+ Qxf6 a3 Nc6 Bd3 d6 Bb5 Qg6 O-O Bh3 Ne1 Be7 f4 Bd7 f5
variations.explanation: The awkward knight jab to b4 is what the books recommend — and almost nobody finds it over the board. Trade on f6 first, put the question with the a-pawn, and after the knight retreats the light-squared bishop swings via d3 to b5, winning back the pawn on your terms. In the corpus this line appears 42 times and scores 69 percent.

variations.name: The …h6 Prophylaxis
variations.pgn: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Nf6 d4 exd4 Nd5 h6 Bf4 Nxd5 exd5 Bb4+ Bd2 Qe7+ Qe2 Bxd2+ Kxd2 Qxe2+ Bxe2
variations.explanation: The quiet pawn move stops any bishop pin on g5 — sensible, and slow. The engine settles the reply: develop the bishop to f4, and when Black simplifies, the endgame after the queen trade is simply more comfortable for White — better development, the d5 space wedge, and a king already active in the centre.

name: Refuting the King’s Gambit (Black)
pgn: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 d5 exd5 Nf6 Bc4 Nxd5 O-O Be6 Qe2 Nc6 d4 Qd6 Nc3 O-O-O Nxd5 Bxd5 Bxd5 Qxd5
uci: e2e4 e7e5 f2f4 e5f4 g1f3 g7g5 h2h4 g5g4 f3e5 g8f6 f1c4 d7d5 e4d5 f8d6
overview: The Modern Defence is the clean, reliable way to meet the King's Gambit. You take the f4-pawn, then strike back with ...d5 — handing the pawn back for a raking lead in development. Instead of clinging to material and getting mated, you turn White's own open lines against him and emerge with the safer king and the better game.
keyIdeas: Answer the gambit with ...d5 — counter-attack the centre, don't hoard the f4-pawn.
Develop before recapturing: ...Nf6 first, then ...Nxd5.
Bring every piece out with tempo (...Be6, ...Nc6) and castle queenside to safety.
Trade into a middlegame where you are better developed, safer, and often still up the pawn.
